newsitem.title: UK: People don't take blood pressure drugs as needed.
newsitem.headline: People don't take blood pressure drugs as needed.

text.p: Patients with high blood pressure are not taking the medicine they need to manage their ailment, partly because of side-effects, researchers reported on Monday.
Dr Wilhelm Vetter, a University of Zurich expert on patient compliance, or willingness to take drugs, said doctors needed to help their patients understand the importance of taking medication.
"Heart attacks and strokes combined are the world's leading killer," said Alberto Zanchetti, former president of the European Society of Hypertension.

"Yet we know from research that at least 50 percent of patients have discontinued treatment with antihypertensive therapy within the first year as a result of side-effects and lack of motivation," he told the European Meeting of Hypertension in Milan.
Their remarks were released in statements issued in London.
The 29-country study was commissioned by the Council for High Blood Pressure Research and partly sponsored by Merck, Sharp and Dohme, the British subsidiary of U.S. drugs giant Merck & Co.
Merck also issued findings showing that patients using its losartan, marketed as Cozaar, were up to 27 percent more likely to take it than patients on other high blood pressure medication.
Losartin is a member of a new class of drugs known as angiotensin II antagonists.

Dr Bernard Bloom of the University of Pennsylvania said 49 percent of patients on losartin took their medication for at least a year, compared to 37 percent of patients on calcium-channel blockers, an older treatment.

Blood pressure medications such as ACE-inhibitors can cause faintness, dry coughing and tiredness. Beta-blockers can lead to wheezing, while calcium channel blockers can trigger constipation and dizziness.
